All companies

How to read this page

This page scores every company in the universe on three things and highlights the few that pass every check. It is generated by six dashboard from the local data store and works offline.

Header

When the data is from (latest price date), how old the latest annual statements are, how many companies are in each branch, and the result of the last six refresh, including any failures.

Filters

Narrow everything on the Dashboard tab: by index (SMI, SMIM or other), peer group, branch, liquid shares only, hiding companies with missing scores, or a ticker/name search. Filters change what you see, never the scores.

Shortlists

Two lists of companies that pass every rule (see "Shortlists and history" below). Each row shows the three scores and the two strongest reasons. A new badge marks companies that joined since the previous run; "since" shows how long a company has been on the list. "Dropped since last run" lists companies that left, with the rule they now fail.

All companies

Every company with its scores. Click a column header to sort. The small coloured number after a score is its change since the previous run. "Mom 12-1" is the share-price return from a year ago to a month ago; "% of 52w high" compares today's price with its highest price of the past year. Coloured dots are warning flags (red keeps a company off the shortlists; hover a dot for details). Click a row to open the company panel.

Company panel

  1. Scores and whether the company is on each list, or the rule it fails.
  2. Why: the metrics that push the scores up (green) or down (red).
  3. Metric breakdown: each metric's value, its percentile among peers and in its branch, the blended percentile used in the score, and its weight. Missing metrics show why they are missing.
  4. Own history: today's main valuation multiple against its value at recent fiscal-year ends. Context only, not part of the score.
  5. Price: five years of weekly prices adjusted for dividends, the 52-week range (shaded).
  6. Flags with explanations.
  7. Key financials: up to four fiscal years in the reporting currency, with CHF below when the company reports in USD or EUR.
  8. Peers: the company against the median of its peer group on five key metrics.

The three scores

Value asks how cheap the company is relative to what it earns, owns and pays out. Quality asks how profitable, cash-generative and financially sound it is. Growth asks how steadily revenue, profits and cash flow have grown. Each score runs from 0 (worst in its comparison group) to 100 (best).

  1. Every metric is ranked as a percentile within the company's branch (general, financials, real estate) and within its peer group.
  2. The two percentiles are blended, giving small peer groups less weight.
  3. A score is the weighted average of its metrics' blended percentiles, using only the metrics available for that company.
  4. If too few metrics are available, the score shows "insufficient data" instead of a number.
Formulas

Percentile: companies with a value are ranked from worst to best; percentile = (rank − 1) ÷ (count − 1) × 100. Ties share the average rank, and a company alone in its group gets 50. Metrics where lower is better are ranked in reverse. Extremes, such as an enterprise value ≤ 0, rank as best or worst as described in the glossary.

Blending: blended = w × peer percentile + (1 − w) × branch percentile, with w = n ÷ (n + ), where n is the number of peers with a value. A peer group of 62 counts about 89%, a group of 5 about 38%.

Score: Σ(weight × blended percentile) ÷ Σ(weights of the available metrics). Minimum metrics: Value , Quality , Growth .

Branches and peer groups

Banks, insurers and property companies can't be judged on the same metrics as an industrial company: a bank's borrowing is its business, and a property company's accounts are dominated by property valuations. So each company sits in a branch, which decides which metrics apply, and in a peer group built from SIX's industry sectors, which decides who it is compared with.

Metric glossary

Every metric used in a score: what it means, how it is computed from the annual statements (using Yahoo's line-item names), whether higher or lower is better, and where it is used with its weight.

Momentum and liquidity

Momentum 12-1 is the dividend-adjusted share-price return from 12 months ago to 1 month ago; the last month is skipped because very recent moves tend to reverse. It needs about 13 months of prices. It is not part of the scores but guards the shortlists: research shows that cheap stocks which keep falling often keep falling.

% of 52-week high is today's close divided by the highest close of the last 252 trading days. A falling knife is a company in the bottom of the universe on momentum that also trades below of its 52-week high.

Liquidity is the median daily value traded over the last three months. Below CHF a share is flagged as thinly traded, and below CHF market cap it is a micro cap. Both keep a company off the shortlists, because its price may move a lot when you buy or sell.

Analyst estimates

Under the scores, each company shows how analysts' earnings-per-share estimate for the current fiscal year (the next year when there is none) changed over the last 90 days, and how many analysts raised or cut it in the last 30 days. The "Est. 90d" column in the table holds the same change. The figures come from Yahoo Finance and are refreshed daily; companies without analyst coverage show "No analyst estimates".

Estimates are not part of the scores. They work like momentum: when analysts are clearly cutting (a fall of or more with more cuts than raises) the company gets an amber estimates_falling flag and is kept off the Growth at a reasonable price list, because that list is a bet on growth expectations. The Value with quality list only shows the warning.

News

Each company panel lists headlines from the last 90 days before the data date, found by searching Google News (Swiss German and French editions) for the company's name. Claude reads each headline once, decides whether it is really about the company (not a namesake or a street) and tags it: warning (losses or profit warning, guidance cut, legal or regulatory trouble, management exit, restructuring or asset sale, capital increase, accounting or auditor issue, delisting, takeover or merger), positive (guidance raise, buyback or dividend, contract or order win) or neutral. Headlines that are not about the company are hidden, as are headlines not yet checked.

A warning headline raises the amber news_warning flag. It is information only: it never takes a company off a shortlist, and the tags are machine-made and can be wrong, so open the article before acting on it.

Warning flags

Red flags keep a company off the shortlists; amber flags are information.

Shortlists and history

Value with quality: Value ≥ and Quality ≥ , no red flag, liquid. Cheap alone isn't enough: cheap companies that are also sound have historically done much better than cheap companies in trouble ("value traps"). Ordered by Value + ½ × Quality.

Growth at a reasonable price: Growth ≥ , Quality ≥ , Value ≥ , growth consistency ≥ , positive 12-1 momentum, share dilution ≤ , no red flag except falling knife, liquid. The Value floor stops this list from filling up with expensive favourites. Ordered by Growth + ½ × Quality.

The Dashboard shows the top of each list. Every run saves the day's scores in data/screener/, and the page compares them with the previous saved run: new marks companies that joined a list, "dropped" lists those that left with the rule they now fail, "since" is the first day of the current unbroken stay on the list, and the small numbers in the table are score changes.

Data and caveats

  • Prices, annual statements and ratios come from Yahoo Finance (unofficial, personal use; the data can contain errors).
  • A fiscal year is used only months after it ends, when annual reports are out. Only annual statements are used, so figures can be more than a year old; the panel shows the statement date.
  • All price-based metrics are in CHF. Companies reporting in USD or EUR are converted: balance-sheet items at the rate on the period end, flows at the average rate of that year. Growth rates use the reporting currency, so currency moves don't count as growth.
  • Earnings mean income from continuing operations, so a gain from selling or spinning off a business doesn't make a company look cheap.
  • Only about four years of statements are available, so growth rates and stability measures rest on few data points. Recent listings have shorter histories.
  • Scores are relative: a high Value score means cheap compared with peers today, not cheap in absolute terms.
  • These are metrics for personal research, not investment advice.
